official.topic: Autism Spectrum Disorder in Young Children: Screening
official.recommendation: The USPSTF concludes that the current evidence is insufficient to assess the balance of benefits and harms of screening for autism spectrum disorder (ASD) in young children for whom no concerns of ASD have been raised by their parents or a clinician.

row.question_original: My 2-year-old seems to be developing normally and nobody has raised any concerns. Should we have him screened for autism?
user_turns: My 2-year-old seems to be developing normally and nobody has raised any concerns. Should we have him screened for autism?
Okay. So bottom line: should I do it or not? Start your answer with exactly one of: DO IT / DON'T / IT DEPENDS.
replies:
Yes, and you don't need to have a concern for it to make sense. The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends that all children be screened for autism at 18 and 24 months, regardless of whether anyone has noticed anything. So if your son is around 2, he's likely due for one, or may have already had it at a well-child visit.

**What screening involves**
- Usually a short parent questionnaire, most often the M-CHAT-R/F, which takes about 5-10 minutes.
- It's often built into the routine 18- or 24-month checkup, so you may have filled one out without it being labeled as an "autism screen."
- You can ask your pediatrician, "Did we do the autism screening, and what were the results?"

**Why do it even if things seem fine**
- Early signs can be subtle, and parents and doctors can miss them, especially in a first child or when a child is otherwise bright or affectionate.
- Early support makes a real difference, so catching things sooner helps.
- A screen isn't a diagnosis. It just flags whether a closer look is worthwhile. Many children who screen positive turn out not to be autistic, and a negative screen is reassuring but not a guarantee.

**Things you can watch for yourself**
- Responds to his name most of the time
- Makes eye contact and shares attention (points to show you things, looks at what you point to)
- Uses or is building words and gestures (waving, pointing)
- Plays back and forth with you, imitates, shows interest in other kids
- Hasn't lost skills he previously had

Differences in any of these don't mean autism, but they're worth mentioning to your doctor.

**Next step**
At his next visit, or by calling the office, ask whether the screening has been done. If it hasn't, ask them to do it. If you ever notice something that worries you between visits, you don't have to wait. You can request an evaluation at any time, and in the US, children under 3 can be evaluated through your state's Early Intervention program without a doctor's referral.

Since he seems to be developing well, the screening will most likely be a quick, reassuring formality.

DO IT. The screening is routine for all children at 18 and 24 months, it takes only a few minutes, and it carries no downside. If your pediatrician already did it at a recent visit, you're covered, so just ask whether it was done and what the result was. If not, ask them to do it at his 24-month checkup.
